sources.title: Akatecos — Etnografía
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas
sources.annotation: Read all substantive ethnographic sections through the research tool. A Mexico-centered account of settlement, local institutions, livelihoods, clothing and public celebrations. Its undated present-tense generalizations are not a current survey. The history section places 1982 events before an ensuing reference to 1981; that sequence is not adopted. Empty headings supply no evidence. An ordinary automated fetch failed, which does not establish a reader paywall.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete substantive webpage text; no linked audio, video or image collection reviewed.

sources.title: Historia y memorias de la comunidad étnica Akateka, volumen II, versión escolar (1997)
sources.publisher: Universidad Rafael Landívar, Instituto de Lingüística; editor Eleuterio Cahuec del Valle
sources.annotation: Selected school-history and memory sections on village relationships, labor and displacement. The PDF copyright is 1997; a separate publisher catalogue says 2016, so no later revision is inferred. A teaching synthesis with narrated memories, not an independently checked chronology. Regional ancient-history claims, dated population figures and sweeping labor or land-law explanations are not adopted here.
sources.contentReviewScope: PDF pp. 3, 6–9, 14–15, 19–24 and 47–50; publisher catalogue records compared. Selected passages, not the complete book.

sources.title: Plan de Desarrollo Municipal y Ordenamiento Territorial: San Miguel Acatán, 2019–2032
sources.publisher: Concejo Municipal de San Miguel Acatán, with SEGEPLAN technical support
sources.annotation: Inspected municipal geography, diagnostic sections and development vision. Documents a 2019 planning process in a municipality identified with the Akateka language community. Proposed services and the 2032 vision are intentions, not verified results. Mixed-year statistics and local estimates are not used as current rates. The report’s evaluative generalizations about residents are not adopted. A municipal jurisdiction is not the whole people’s homeland.
sources.contentReviewScope: PDF pp. 1–3, 10, 14–15, 26, 28, 30–31 and 52, plus selected web-rendered education passages; no complete implementation audit.

sources.title: Tz’ib’b’il Qichmam Akateka: Literatura Maya Akateka (2020)
sources.publisher: Comunidad Lingüística Akateka — Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala; Carlos Francisco Francisco, translator
sources.annotation: Read credits, presentation, both teaching guides and contents. A community publication for language learning; its introduction explicitly describes ten adapted and translated narratives. The guides distinguish first-language revitalization and second-language learning and involve proficient speakers. This supports an account of educational aims and methods, not measured success, a census of children’s language use, or a claim that every story originated uniquely among Akateko people.
sources.contentReviewScope: PDF pp. 1–13; selected opening Akateko pages inspected for format only. No independent translation, complete story reading, audio or teaching-outcome evaluation.

supportingSources.title: Akateko — Catálogo de las Lenguas Indígenas Nacionales
supportingSources.annotation: Complete short language/locality table inspected. Records Kuti’ and named localities in Campeche, Chiapas and Quintana Roo. Useful orientation and naming evidence, kept outside the substantive target because it is a brief catalogue listing. It does not establish all settlements, current population, a homeland boundary or one government.
supportingSources.contentReviewScope: Complete short table and heading; the catalogue’s linked wider documentation is not counted as separately read.

proposedSections.title: A people, a language and several local settings
proposedSections.text: Akateko is a Maya people and language name. INPI records Kuti’ as a self-designation. A Guatemalan school history places communities around San Miguel Acatán, San Rafael La Independencia and Jo’om. These descriptions neither draw fixed boundaries nor establish a single government. Akateko and Awakateko require separate reading paths.

proposedSections.title: Reading a history alongside community memory
proposedSections.text: The Landívar school volume combines regional history with narrated community memories. It connects San Miguel Acatán and San Rafael La Independencia and describes their separation into municipalities in 1924. Its historical account follows changing labor demands and later wartime displacement. Read it as a dated teaching synthesis: memories and regional summaries invite comparison with original records. The PDF carries a 1997 copyright even though another catalogue lists 2016. Neither date makes its population figures current.

proposedSections.title: Local institutions in Chiapas
proposedSections.text: INPI’s ethnography distinguishes municipal agency roles from ejido land administration in La Gloria. It also describes religious diversity and public San Miguel celebrations connecting settlements with Guatemala. These are accounts of particular Mexican communities, not a universal institutional or religious pattern. The source’s discussion of clothing links changing use to security, cost and migration; dress should be understood through those histories rather than as an unchanging test of identity.

proposedSections.title: Literature as a teaching resource
proposedSections.text: The Akateka language community’s 2020 literary publication sets out separate approaches for first-language revitalization and second-language learners. Its guides connect oral storytelling, proficient speakers, reading and writing. The introduction describes adapted and translated narratives rather than claiming an exclusively Akateko origin for every story. This is evidence of community educational work and stated teaching methods; publication alone does not demonstrate how many classrooms used the material or what learners achieved.

proposedSections.title: A dated municipal view of priorities
proposedSections.text: San Miguel Acatán’s 2019–2032 development plan offers a local-government perspective. Its diagnosis discusses school access, water and health services, alongside agriculture and markets. It identifies infrastructure and economic opportunities while proposing future improvements. The 2032 vision is a planning goal, not an achieved condition. Municipal statistics mix years and some schooling estimates are attributed to local officials; they should not be treated as current community-wide rates. This document concerns one jurisdiction rather than every Akateko settlement.

proposedSections.title: Using a locality catalogue carefully
proposedSections.text: INALI lists Kuti’ under Akateko and supplies localities in Chiapas, Campeche and Quintana Roo, including La Gloria, Maya Tecún I and Maya Balam. The table helps a reader follow names into more detailed research. A short language catalogue cannot establish a complete population count, the extent of historical homelands, or political equivalence among the listed communities.

evidenceNotes: INPI ethnic name and INALI linguistic self-name have distinct institutional scopes. Neither is adopted as the only self-designation everywhere.
PDF history copyright is 1997. Publisher record pb=109 also gives 1997; pb=565 gives 2016. Count the inspected work once and disclose the discrepancy.
Do not adopt INPI chronology that narrates 1982 events then calls resulting movement 1981. Scholarly displacement studies supply better scoped histories.
2019 municipal plan contains mixed-year projections, qualitative local estimates and broad evaluative explanations. No current poverty, health, school completion or speaker percentages are inferred.
Public teaching literature has adapted pan-Maya narratives. No uniquely Akateko story provenance is inferred; no restricted ritual content is reproduced.
